title: Approximating Areas
lead: The area under a curve is approached through the areas of rectangles standing on a partition of the interval, each as tall as the function at one point of its subinterval. Sigma notation writes such sums compactly; the choice of point gives the left-endpoint and right-endpoint approximations, the upper and lower sums and the Riemann sums, whose limit defines the area under the curve.
objectives: Use sigma (summation) notation to calculate sums and powers of integers.
Use the sum of rectangular areas to approximate the area under a curve.
Use Riemann sums to approximate area.
summary_html:
• The use of sigma (summation) notation of the form $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}$ is useful for expressing long sums of values in compact form.
  • For a continuous function defined over an interval $[a,b],$ the process of dividing the interval into n equal parts, extending a rectangle to the graph of the function, calculating the areas of the series of rectangles, and then summing the areas yields an approximation of the area of that region.
  • The width of each rectangle is $\Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n}.$
  • Riemann sums are expressions of the form $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \kf(x_{i}^{*})\Delta x,$ and can be used to estimate the area under the curve $y=\kf(x).$ Left- and right-endpoint approximations are special kinds of Riemann sums where the values of $\{x_{i}^{*}\}$ are chosen to be the left or right endpoints of the subintervals, respectively.
  • Riemann sums allow for much flexibility in choosing the set of points $\{x_{i}^{*}\}$ at which the function is evaluated, often with an eye to obtaining a lower sum or an upper sum.

exercises.prompt: Let $d_{j}$ denote the hours of daylight and $\delta_{j}$ denote the increase in the hours of daylight from day $j-1$ to day j in Fargo, North Dakota, on the jth day of the year. Interpret $d_{1}+\sum_{j=2}^{365} \delta_{j}.$

answer.solution: Each $\delta_{j}$ is $d_{j}-d_{j-1},$ so the sum telescopes: $d_{1}+\sum_{j=2}^{365}\delta_{j}=d_{1}+(d_{2}-d_{1})+(d_{3}-d_{2})+\cdots+(d_{365}-d_{364})=d_{365}.$ It is the number of hours of daylight in Fargo on day 365, the last day of the year.

exercises.prompt: To help get in shape, Joe gets a new pair of running shoes. If Joe runs 1 mi each day in week 1 and adds $\frac{1}{10}$ mi to his daily routine each week, what is the total mileage on Joe’s shoes after 25 weeks?

answer.solution: The total mileage is $7\;\times \;\sum_{i=1}^{25} (1+\frac{(i-1)}{10})=7\;\times \;25+\frac{7}{10}\;\times \;12\;\times \;25=385\;\text{mi}.$

[T] $y=x^{4}-5x^{2}+4$ on the interval $[-2,2],$ which has an exact area of $\frac{32}{15}$
Explain why, if $\kf(a)\ge0$ and $\kf$ is increasing on $[a,b],$ that the left endpoint estimate is a lower bound for the area below the graph of $\kf$ on $[a,b].$

answer.solution: If $[c,d]$ is a subinterval of $[a,b]$ under one of the left-endpoint sum rectangles, then the area of the rectangle contributing to the left-endpoint estimate is $\kf(c)(d-c).$ But, $\kf(c)\le \kf(x)$ for $c\le x\le d,$ so the area under the graph of $\kf$ between c and d is $\kf(c)(d-c)$ plus the area below the graph of $\kf$ but above the horizontal line segment at height $\kf(c),$ which is positive. As this is true for each left-endpoint sum interval, it follows that the left Riemann sum is less than or equal to the area below the graph of $\kf$ on $[a,b].$

exercises.prompt: Explain why, if $\kf(b)\ge0$ and $\kf$ is decreasing on $[a,b],$ that the left endpoint estimate is an upper bound for the area below the graph of $\kf$ on $[a,b].$

answer.solution: Since $\kf$ is decreasing and $\kf(b)\ge 0,$ $\kf(x)\ge 0$ on all of $[a,b].$ On each subinterval $[x_{i-1},x_{i}]$ the largest value of $\kf$ is $\kf(x_{i-1}),$ at the left endpoint, so the rectangle of height $\kf(x_{i-1})$ contains the region below the graph over that subinterval. Adding over the subintervals, the left-endpoint estimate is at least the area below the graph on $[a,b]:$ it is an upper bound.

exercises.prompt: Show that, in general, $\kR_{N}-\kL_{N}=(b-a)\;\times \;\frac{\kf(b)-\kf(a)}{N}.$

answer.solution: $\kL_{N}=\frac{b-a}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \kf(a+(b-a)\frac{i-1}{N})=\frac{b-a}{N}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \kf(a+(b-a)\frac{i}{N})$ and $\kR_{N}=\frac{b-a}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \kf(a+(b-a)\frac{i}{N}).$ The left sum has a term corresponding to $i=0$ and the right sum has a term corresponding to $i=N.$ In $\kR_{N}-\kL_{N},$ any term corresponding to $i=1,2,\ldots,N-1$ occurs once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so each such term cancels and one is left with $\kR_{N}-\kL_{N}=\frac{b-a}{N}(\kf(a+(b-a))\frac{N}{N})-(\kf(a)+(b-a)\frac{0}{N})=\frac{b-a}{N}(\kf(b)-\kf(a)).$

exercises.prompt: Explain why, if $\kf$ is increasing on $[a,b],$ the error between either $\kL_{N}$ or $\kR_{N}$ and the area $\kA$ below the graph of $\kf$ is at most $(b-a)\frac{\kf(b)-\kf(a)}{N}.$

answer.solution: For an increasing $\kf,$ the left-endpoint rectangles lie under the graph and the right-endpoint rectangles cover it, so $\kL_{N}\le\kA\le\kR_{N}.$ The area therefore differs from either sum by at most $\kR_{N}-\kL_{N}.$ The two sums share every term but one at each end: $\kR_{N}$ has $\kf(b)\frac{b-a}{N}$ where $\kL_{N}$ has $\kf(a)\frac{b-a}{N},$ so $\kR_{N}-\kL_{N}=(b-a)\frac{\kf(b)-\kf(a)}{N},$ the bound claimed.

exercises.prompt:
For each of the three graphs:

  1. Obtain a lower bound $L(\kA)$ for the area enclosed by the curve by adding the areas of the squares enclosed completely by the curve.
  2. Obtain an upper bound $U(\kA)$ for the area by adding to $L(\kA)$ the areas $B(\kA)$ of the squares enclosed partially by the curve.
In the previous exercise, explain why $L(\kA)$ gets no smaller while $U(\kA)$ gets no larger as the squares are subdivided into four boxes of equal area.

answer.solution: When each square is cut into four boxes of equal area, a square that was enclosed completely gives four boxes that are all enclosed completely, so every area counted in $L(\kA)$ is still counted, and boxes cut from partially enclosed squares may be added: $L(\kA)$ gets no smaller. Every box counted in $U(\kA)$ after the cut lies in a square that was counted before, since a box that touches the region lies in a square that touched it, so $U(\kA)$ gets no larger.

figure.alt: A wedge of a circle cut at an acute angle theta = 2pi / n. Several extra lines are drawn. The first is a line A connecting the ends of the two radii, creating a triangle. The second is another line B parallel to the A, connecting the radii a few units in from each endpoint. A concentric curve C connects the endpoints of B and is tangent to A near its midpoint. The area between this curve C and the edge of the circle is shaded in pink, and the rest of the wedge is purple. A final concentric curve is drawn very close to angle theta.

exercises.prompt: A unit circle is made up of n wedges equivalent to the inner wedge in the figure. The base of the inner triangle is 1 unit and its height is $\sin(\frac{2\pi}{n}).$ The base of the outer triangle is $B=\cos(\frac{\pi}{n})+\sin(\frac{\pi}{n})\tan(\frac{\pi}{n})$ and the height is $H=B\;\sin(\frac{2\pi}{n}).$ Use this information to argue that the area of a unit circle is equal to π.

answer.solution: Let $\kA$ be the area of the unit circle. The circle encloses n congruent triangles each of area $\frac{\sin(\frac{2\pi}{n})}{2},$ so $\frac{n}{2}\sin(\frac{2\pi}{n})\le \kA.$ Similarly, the circle is contained inside n congruent triangles each of area $\frac{BH}{2}=\frac{1}{2}{(cos(\frac{\pi}{n})+sin(\frac{\pi}{n})tan(\frac{\pi}{n}))}^{2}sin(\frac{2\pi}{n}),$ so $\kA\le\frac{n}{2}\sin(\frac{2\pi}{n})(\cos(\frac{\pi}{n})+\sin(\frac{\pi}{n})\tan{(\frac{\pi}{n}))}^{2}.$ As $n\to \infty,\frac{n}{2}\sin(\frac{2\pi}{n})=\frac{\;\sin(\frac{2\pi}{n})}{(\frac{2}{n})}Α\to \pi,$ so we conclude $\pi\le \kA.$ Also, as $n\to \infty,\cos(\frac{\pi}{n})+\sin(\frac{\pi}{n})\tan(\frac{\pi}{n})\to 1,$ so we also have $\kA\le\pi.$ By the squeeze theorem for limits, we conclude that $\kA=\pi.$
